title: Heart Health: Risk Factors and Prevention
content:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) — which includes coronary artery disease, heart attack, and stroke — is the leading cause of death globally. Most CVD is preventable through lifestyle modification and, where necessary, medical management of risk factors.

Major modifiable risk factors:

High blood pressure (hypertension): Damages artery walls over time, making the heart work harder. Controlled with lifestyle changes (reduced salt, regular exercise, weight loss) and/or medication. Target below 130/80 mmHg for most adults.

High LDL cholesterol: Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol deposits in artery walls, forming plaques that can restrict blood flow or rupture and cause a heart attack or stroke. Lifestyle changes (reducing saturated fat, increasing fibre) lower LDL; statins are highly effective medications when lifestyle alone is insufficient.

Type 2 diabetes: High blood glucose damages blood vessels and nerves over time. Well-controlled blood sugar reduces cardiovascular risk.

Smoking: Damages blood vessel walls, reduces oxygen in blood, raises heart rate and blood pressure, and accelerates plaque formation. Quitting at any age reduces risk — within 1 year of quitting, heart attack risk drops significantly.

Physical inactivity: Regular aerobic activity strengthens the heart muscle, lowers blood pressure, improves cholesterol, and helps maintain healthy weight.

Obesity and overweight: Excess body fat — particularly visceral (abdominal) fat — is associated with elevated blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood glucose.

Warning signs of a heart attack: chest discomfort (pressure, squeezing, fullness, or pain); discomfort in the arms, back, neck, jaw, or stomach; shortness of breath; cold sweat, nausea, or lightheadedness. Symptoms in women may be subtler — fatigue, jaw pain, and nausea are common.

If you suspect a heart attack, call emergency services immediately (112 in India, 911 in the US). Do not drive yourself to the hospital. Chewing one regular-strength aspirin (325 mg) while awaiting emergency services may help if the person is not allergic and has no other contraindications — but emergency services should be contacted first.

Warning signs of stroke (use FAST): Face drooping on one side; Arm weakness (ask person to raise both arms — does one drift down?); Speech difficulty (slurred, strange, or unable to speak); Time to call emergency services immediately.
source: Original — based on American Heart Association public education materials and CDC Heart Disease facts (public domain summaries)
